scenario: Read a grocery cereal shelf from photos
did: List every cereal on the shelves with its average price into a spreadsheet.
why: The spreadsheet correctly lists Golden Grahams, Krave Chocolate, Cocoa Krispies and Fruity Pebbles — all four are clearly on the shelves in the photos. But the rubric subtracts points for including them, as if they shouldn't be there, so a correct reading gets marked wrong.
fix: Remove the four checks that penalize listing Golden Grahams, Krave Chocolate, Cocoa Krispies and Fruity Pebbles. If you want an "absent product" trap, base it on a cereal that genuinely isn't on any shelf.

scenario: Source computer parts on Amazon for a gift
did: Find each product (or a valid alternative), record the link and price, and update a savings sheet.
why: The task lets the agent choose the exact product or a valid alternative, yet ten checks each demand one specific Amazon price or total. Any equally-valid alternative has different prices, so a perfectly good answer fails those checks.
fix: Change those ten checks to confirm the agent's own numbers are consistent — the recorded prices match the products it actually chose, the estimated total equals the sum of the rows, and the projected balance equals savings minus the total — instead of requiring one fixed price.

scenario: Audit and organize a batch of social-media content drafts
did: Sort the thumbnail drafts by pillar, apply the brand rules, schedule them, and log the work.
why: Several checks pack multiple separate requirements into one line, so a partly-correct answer can't be scored fairly. For example, one passes only if all six different sources were consulted; another rolls two unrelated scheduling rules together; another lists six different things that must all appear in MEMORY.md.
fix: Split those bundled checks so each tests one thing — one per source consulted, one per scheduling rule, one per file action, and one per item that must be kept in MEMORY.md.

scenario: Rebuild a social-media plan from a handwritten planning note
did: Recreate the plan, flag where the posts don't match it, and email the findings.
why: Most of the rubric is solid. One check asks the agent to flag the June 22 dashboard post as wrong for saying June 24 "instead of July 1." But the planning note sets the dashboard for June 24 — July 1 is the support-maintenance date, not the dashboard — so that check would mark a correct answer wrong.
fix: Remove the dashboard/July-1 part of that email check (June 24 is correct). Also correct two filenames in the rubric to match the actual file, final viasual.png.

scenario: Audit a home renovation against the invoices and plans
did: Write a discrepancy report comparing invoiced work, payments, and what was actually done.
why: The rubric is mostly sound. One check combines two different jobs into one line — totaling the invoiced amounts and sorting the work by what's visually confirmed — so the two can't be judged separately.
fix: Split that check into two: one for the invoice totals, one for the visual-confirmation categorization.

scenario: Review a real-estate listing and write a memo
did: Check the listing's numbers and produce a memo.
why: The rubric is mostly sound. One check bundles two separate expectations — that the memo logs every step taken and that it records the per-section item counts — so a memo could do one but not the other and still can't be scored cleanly.
fix: Split it into two checks: one for the activity log, one for the per-section counts.
